fixes.explanation: Athens is a good guess, friend, but it's not the city Paul names here. He says, "After I have been there, I must see Rome as well." (Acts 19:21) Rome is the city he names after Jerusalem.

That's right. Timothy and Erastus go ahead to Macedonia, while Paul "…stayed for a time in the province of Asia." (Acts 19:22) Timothy is one of Paul's helpers, and so is Erastus. Paul sends them off, and he stays put for a time.

Not yet, friend. Paul has Jerusalem in his plans (Acts 19:21), but this verse says he stayed for a time in the province of Asia. At this point in the passage, Jerusalem is only what he has resolved to do. Hold your horses, baker.
Business is the word. The silver shrines of Artemis bring "…much business to the craftsmen." (Acts 19:24) Demetrius is the silversmith who makes them. The text says much business, not a little.

Fame sounds fancy, but that's not the word. The verse says the shrines bring "…much business to the craftsmen." (Acts 19:24) Demetrius is a silversmith who makes them. It's business the verse names, not fame.

Silas is a fun name to throw out, friend, but Demetrius never says it. He has gathered the craftsmen and the workmen in related trades (Acts 19:25), and he points at just one man. "…this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away." (Acts 19:26)

True. Demetrius says of Paul, "He says that man-made gods are no gods at all." (Acts 19:26) That's Demetrius describing Paul's message to the craftsmen and the workmen in related trades he gathered (Acts 19:25). I bet that message did not go over well with people whose business was shrines.

Shouting it is. "When the men heard this, they were enraged and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:28) Demetrius finished talking, and the volume went straight up. Their first move after hearing him is to shout.
That's a calm idea, and these men are anything but calm. The text says they "…were enraged and began shouting…" (Acts 19:28) Closing shops isn't what the verse says they do. Shouting is.

Good guess, but it isn't what the text says. They "…were enraged and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:28) The shouting comes first, and going after Paul isn't in this verse. The next verse shows the whole city in disarray.

Those two are Paul's helpers, and Paul sent them ahead to Macedonia (Acts 19:22). But the crowd drags into the theatre "…Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s traveling companions from Macedonia." (Acts 19:29) Those are the two names the verse gives.

False is right. "Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples would not allow him." (Acts 19:30) The disciples did not allow him to go before the assembly. I think that was a good friend move.

Yes, officials of the province of Asia. "Even some of Paul’s friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre." (Acts 19:31) They didn't just ask, they begged. These are friends of Paul who hold office in the province.

Not at all, friend. The text says "…most of them did not even know why they were there." (Acts 19:32) Some were shouting one thing and some another. That means most of the people in the theatre didn't know the reason they were there.

False is right. "Some were shouting one thing and some another, and most of them did not even know why they were there." (Acts 19:32) That says most of them, not every last person. A lot of people shouting, and most of them not knowing why.

No bowing in this passage, friend. Alexander "…motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people." (Acts 19:33) The Jews in the crowd had just pushed him forward. Pushed to the front of a loud crowd, and the first thing he asks for is quiet. I think that takes nerve.

That's right. "…when they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted in unison for about two hours: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:34) Alexander had motioned for silence so he could make his defense (Acts 19:33). What the verse records next is two hours of the same shout.

The text doesn't say that, friend. It says "…when they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted in unison for about two hours: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:34) Alexander had motioned for silence to make his defense (Acts 19:33). The verse records two hours of shouting.

True. After the city clerk quieted the crowd, he declared, "…doesn’t everyone know that the city of Ephesus is guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image, which fell from heaven?" (Acts 19:35) He's reminding them of something he says everyone knows. The quieting comes first, and then he speaks.

The courts are right. The clerk says, "…the courts are open and proconsuls are available. Let them bring charges against one another there." (Acts 19:38) A proconsul is a Roman governor. That's where he points Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen if they have a complaint.

Secret would be a surprise, friend. The clerk says, "…it must be settled in a legal assembly." (Acts 19:39) Legal is the word he uses, and secret never shows up. That's where he says anything beyond the courts must go.

Treason sounds heavier, friend, but the clerk never says it. He says, "…we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today’s events…" (Acts 19:40) Notice the "we," so he counts himself in on the jeopardy. I think that's one worried clerk.

That's right. "After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly." (Acts 19:41) First the clerk quieted the crowd (Acts 19:35), then he spoke, and then he dismissed them. Before that, they had shouted for about two hours (Acts 19:34).

Nope, friend. The disciples would not allow Paul to go before the assembly (Acts 19:30), and his friends who were officials begged him not to venture into the theatre (Acts 19:31). After the clerk's speech, "…he dismissed the assembly." (Acts 19:41) Nobody sends for Paul in this passage.
